analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal cigarette tax to 32 cents a pack and deposits the extra revenue into Medicare's hospital trust fund.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it was referred to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, drew zero cosponsors, and died there when the 103rd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have raised the federal excise tax on cigarettes from 24 cents to 32 cents per pack, effective October 1993. Every dollar of the additional tax would have been deposited into Medicare's Hospital Insurance Trust Fund, which pays hospital bills for seniors and disabled people. It also imposed a one-time tax on cigarettes in warehouses and stores when the increase took effect, with a small credit and an exemption for small stockpiles. The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and never went anywhere.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare's Hospital Insurance Trust Fund would have gained a dedicated new revenue stream from the higher tax, helping it pay hospital bills for seniors. Public health would have benefited indirectly, since higher cigarette prices are known to reduce smoking, especially among young people.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal cigarette excise tax to 32 cents per pack (16 dollars per thousand small cigarettes), up from the 24-cent rate, with the increase applying to cigarettes removed after September 30, 1993.
Deposits all revenue from the tax increase into the Federal Hospital Insurance Trust Fund, the Medicare account that pays for hospital care, transferred monthly from the general Treasury fund.

Imposes a one-time floor-stock tax on cigarettes in inventory when the increase takes effect, with a 30,000-cigarette exemption for small holders and a 60-dollar credit, so the tax reaches product already on shelves rather than only new production.

analysis.who_pays: Smokers, who would pay about 8 cents more per pack, a burden that falls hardest on lower-income people because smoking is more common among them. Cigarette manufacturers, wholesalers, and retailers would bear the one-time tax on inventory and would face lower sales as prices rose.

drawbacks.text: Cigarette taxes are regressive: the roughly 8-cents-per-pack increase takes a larger share of income from a low-wage smoker than from a wealthy one, so the new Medicare revenue would be paid disproportionately by working people who smoke.

The one-time floor-stock tax would immediately hit wholesalers and retailers holding inventory on the effective date, though the bill softens this with an exemption for people holding 30,000 cigarettes or fewer and a 60-dollar credit for others.
The bill dedicates the revenue to Medicare but does nothing to help the smokers who would fund it, offering no cessation programs or other offsetting benefit.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a straightforward trade: a modest regressive tax on a harmful product, with the money earmarked for Medicare's hospital fund. Higher cigarette prices do reduce smoking, particularly among teenagers, so there is a real public-health side benefit alongside the revenue. The main honest objection is that the burden falls on low-income smokers rather than on broad ability to pay, and the bill provides nothing for the people paying it. On balance it is a defensible, if narrow, piece of public-health and Medicare-financing policy.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Andrew Jacobs Jr. of Indiana introduced the bill on January 26, 1993.
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee with jurisdiction over tax bills.
No further action was ever recorded; it never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco manufacturers and retailers are better off because the tax increase never happened, and smokers avoided the higher price. Medicare's trust fund never received the new revenue.

for.name: Rep. Andrew Jacobs Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and offered it alone, with no cosponsors.

against.name: House Committee on Ways and Means
against.role: The tax-writing committee, chaired by Rep. Dan Rostenkowski (D-IL)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill had a single Democratic sponsor with zero cosponsors from either party, so the partisan shape of any potential support is unknown.

industries.note: The higher tax would raise cigarette prices and the one-time floor-stock tax would hit existing inventory, cutting sales. Higher prices reduce smoking, so the industry's loss in this bill was the public's health gain.

They would owe the one-time tax on cigarettes held for sale on October 1, 1993, payable by March 1994, with a 30,000-cigarette exemption and a 60-dollar credit cushioning small holders. Retail prices would rise, reducing sales.
